The announcement was passed through the visual effects industry in much the same manner as an old comedy routine. "There's good news and bad news. The good news is that Paramount is going to make a new version of Star Trek for television. The bad news is that they're going to use video to generate all the effects." This revelation was greeted with knowing smiles from the cognoscenti. Horror stories related to video compositing abound and are traded like lurid campfire tales amongst he stam television producers. One needed to look no further than such low-end series as Logan's Run and Land of the Lost - or even the new Twilight Zone - to realize that video effects still had a long way to go before matching the quality of film. Recalling these recent and largely unsuccessful attempts at creating video magic, the effects community chuckled collectively and returned to work secure in the knowledge that once again film would emerge as the firmly-entrenched medium of choice. It was a position that had been bolstered by the multitude of effects companies that had risen from the visual renaissance of the post Star Wars and Close Encounters era. Utilizing the techniques introduced by these landmark productions, feature quality optical effects were now available for television - a far cry from the dismal state of affairs that prevailed when the Star Trek series was first introduced in 1966. Every major studio had maintained its own effects department until the hard times of the 1960s forced many of them to disband their permanent staffs. The resulting lacuna was filled by the formation of several privately owned companies which subsequently provided the majority of effects for films and television. Prior to Star Trek, most television effects work consisted of standard optical fare such as titles, fades, dissolves and the occasional laser beam, lightning bolt or matte painting. When Gene Roddenberry conceived his groundbreaking series he was undoubtedly aware of the lethargic state of the effects business, but even he was aghast to discover that it would take the combined efforts of every major effects company in Hollywood to meet the demands of his show. Most of the effects in Star Trek were unique, custom-made and quite bold for their time. Images now taken for granted - multicolored phaser blasts, sparkling transporter beams, exotic ships in orbit around spinning planets and glowing energy creatures - were unthinkably expensive luxuries for a mere television show. Yet every week, viewers were treated to as many of these flashy spectacles as Roddenberry could afford. As a result, the standard of effects generated specifically for television reached a high point, only to drop several notches upon cancellation of the show. Noting the reemergence of science fiction and its enormous popularity in feature films, television predictably followed suit with the production of such futuristic programs as Battlestar Galacticaand Buck Rogers. Advances in bluescreen technology and motion control - advances which drastically reduced costs - convinced many producers that the time had finally arrived for the application of feature film-style effects to television. Unfortunately, the number of shots demanded by studios negated any savings. Galactica and Buck Rogers came in at nearly $1 million per episode, with a significant chunk of that money dedicated to effects production. The renaissance was not as remunerative as had been hoped. It is one of the ironies of modern television production that once effects could be generated faster and reused, producers began to cut schedules and budgets accordingly. All of these facts weighed heavily on Gene Roddenberry and Paramount Pictures as they began assembling a team to resurrect their twenty-year-old television series, prompting them to create not only a new generation of characters, but a new generation of special effects as well. As might be expected in an age when mere wristwatches are multifunction computers, state-of-the-art technology was to play a pivotal role in this new approach to visual effects for television - an approach that would apply the latest advances in both film and video. "To try to do the kinds of effects we are doing and meet the schedule we are faced with would be impossible to do on film alone," asserted Peter Lauritson, associate producer for Star Trek - The Next Generation. "When the idea to bring back Star Trek came up, I started investigating how they had done the effects on the old series - because the time constraints of weekly television are very difficult. As it turns out, the original show had every optical house in town working for them and they were right up against their schedule every single week. I had been following the advances of videotape for some time and felt that the timing was right to use video postproduction for this series. It was feasible and it was the only way this show would fly and not be an absolute killer to the people working on it. One of the things I had to do was bring to everyone's attention the fact that if we went with video, we would never be able to release the show on film. That was a big issue for the studio." Indeed, for Paramount this meant the potential loss of millions of dollars in revenue since often a television series broadcast free in the United States is recut and several episodes combined into feature form for overseas theatrical release. Finishing the new Star Trek series on video meant that the shows would have to be transferred from video to either film or foreign video format - an unhappy situation acerbated by the differences in video resolution between the United States and the rest of the world. Clearly the low resolution of American video would produce unacceptably inferior copies in every other format - roughly the equivalent of trying to make 35mm or 70mm optical blowups from 16mm film. Faced with the facts, Paramount had to reconcile the potential loss of revenue before they would proceed with video compositing, "They hesitated," Lauritson recalled, "but when they saw the difference between a film budget and a video budget for the series, it did not take long to convince them that this was the only way it was ever going to work." Though the live-action sequences for Star Trek - The Next Generation are shot on 35mm film - as are almost all of the elements involved in the creation of the effects sequences - everything is ultimately transferred to videotape for final presentation. With an average of fifty to sixty effects shots per episode - sometimes as many as one hundred - the ten- to twelve-day turnaround schedule for effects would be unimaginable for a film-based facility. "Everything we do with video can also be done with film," Lauritson explained, "but not within the time limitations of our show. The world of video has made great strides in the past few years and that is what has made this show possible. The ability to transfer film elements to video, manipulate them electronically and output an effect that maintains the look of film is what gives us the edge." Two companies share primary responsibility for providing the new Star Trek with that 'edge' - The Post Group and Composite Image Systems. Both have distinguished themselves as pioneers in video postproduction, offering state-of-the-art equipment and a notable commitment to film-quality visuals. The bulk of the effects work is performed by The Post Group -a Hollywood company which boasts fifteen video editing bays, a small motion control and insert stage, a computer graphics center and an audio department. While The Post Group produces most of the show's flashy eye-grabbing effects, Composite Image Systems handles the essential film-to-video transfers and most of the bluescreen compositing. In addition to securing the services of two top-notch effects facilities, Lauritson was faced with finding an effects supervisor to oversee the pilot and subsequent shows. Requiring a hybrid background that included both film effects and video compositing - a key qualification most applicants failed to meet - the position was not an easy one to fill. Selected at last was veteran effects director Robert Legato, who had the requisite hands-on experience with videotape compositing as a result of his commercial work at Robert Abel Associates. Even with his strong background in conventional camera and video, Legato was surprised at the scope of effects required for any given script. "No one anticipated that the series would be quite this much work," Legato admitted. "The two-hour pilot alone had more than two hundred special effects - which is equivalent to a feature film. In our first season, we did about eighteen hundred effects in less than eight months - solely due to our ability to operate in the domain of video. Even though our visuals are not always as complex as those in film, the amount of work is staggering." So much so, in fact, that a second effects supervisor - Dan Curry - was enlisted a few weeks into the first season to share with Legato the task of overseeing both the on-set 35mm plate photography related to effects and the subsequent postproduction video work. Legato teams with coordinator Gary Hutzel and effects editor Stan Kellam while Curry works with coordinator Ron Moore and editor Peter Moyer. Both Curry and Moore are seasoned alumni of film effects houses - Curry as director of creative services at Cinema Research Corporation and Moore as an optical cameraman and effects editor at Boss Film Corporation. Strong film backgrounds are crucial to the specialized effects work that Star Trek requires - combining film tricks of the trade with the awesome technology wielded on video by The Post Group and Composite Image Systems. "We get the scripts without storyboards," noted Curry, "so I make up the storyboards myself. It makes it a lot easier to put a shot together when everybody has an idea of what we are looking for. Ninety percent of our effects begin as film elements which are then transferred and manipulated on video." Even the beloved starship Enterprise exists primarily as a collection of Vistavision film elements which are transferred and composited as needed. Industrial Light and Magic constructed the new Enterprise for the pilot show and also provided about forty reusable bluescreen elements of it - most of them generic flybys and establishing scenes - as well as some upto-date multiplane starfield backgrounds pioneered by the original Star Trek series. "ILM was also instrumental in providing us with the rubber band warp-out effect," Legato stated. "Though it looks like a video effect, it was done on film. The idea is that the Enterprise stretches out or elongates as it goes into warp drive. Then, as it reaches its speed, it snaps back like a rubber band and goes off into the distance. I read that Doug Trumbull had tried to do something similar on Star Trek - The Motion Picture, but was unable to get it together in time. No one had ever slitscanned a three-dimensional model before and he encountered terrible problems using a literal slit moving in front of his camera lens. I came up with the alternate idea of scanning a slit of light across a two-foot model. The camera would be positioned very close to the tail of the Enterprise while a projected sliver of light swept across the surface from the rear to the front. As the light scanned forward, the camera would open its shutter and begin to move away, streaking the image onto the film. By the time the camera reached the end

of its track, the sliver of light had reached the front of the Enterprise - now fifteen feet away and very tiny in the frame - creating the effect of a stretched starship. By repositioning the start and stop points of the camera, the image of the interprise could be made to literally stretch and collapse on demand." Since streaking is an inherently expensive technique - requiring several minutes per frame and tying up valuable camera and stage time for hours or even days - only three different warp drive shots were created. These film elements - along with more traditional shots of the Enterprise - are transferred as needed by Composite Image Systems and composited electronically by The Post Group. As straightforward as it may seem, the technology is relatively new. Thirty years ago there was no question that film and video were two very distinct and different media. Video was live; film was recorded. There was no overlapping. It was not until 1956 that Ampex introduced the first commercially successful videotape recorder - but even then, there was no such thing as videotape editing, Industry experts predicted a short life for the new marvel. As far as they could see, there would be no way ever to edit videotape - which was, after all, made up of invisible magnetic frames separated by bands only a few thousandths of an inch wide. In response to this dire forecast, Ampex developed a basic editing methodology that involved the introduction of magnetic marks - called edit pulses - on the edge of the tape. These edit pulses indicated the locations of the diagonal frame lines and were made visible by exposing the tape to a chemical solution. A skilled video editor wielding a razor blade could cut the tape precisely at the frame line while it was held in place mechanically, It was a slow and meticulous cutting process similar to the way film is edited even today. Video editing remained in this primitive state until the introduction of time code systems in the late 1960s. When time code was introduced, it was viewed as an electronic equivalent to the edge numbers on film. Time code identified each and every video frame uniquely by hour, minute, second and frame - acting in a sense as electronic sprocket holes. In 1970, the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers acted to establish a time code standard that would provide for interchangability of equipment made by different manufacturers - a standard which exists to this day as the basis for all video synchronization and editing. Electronic editing was just around the corner. At its most basic, electronic editing involves a videotape source and a videotape recorder - both of which have to be rolling for a scene to be edited onto a master tape. The first editing systems using SMPTE time code were able to meet the desperate need for one machine to control both the source and record units, making them the standard for video postproduction at the time. But the stage was already being set for a new kind of video technology. The impact of the computer was beginning to be felt by the video industry. formed the CMX Corporation with the idea of merging a computer and an editing system to create a computerized electronic videotape editor. The overall intent was to produce a device capable of random access storage of images, thus allowing video editors to view and rearrange their decisions without having to record or splice anything on tape. The resulting CMX 600 was an editing system without peer for its time. Because of its complexity and cost, however, it was used on only a limited basis and has long been out of production. But the technology unleashed by its development - the idea that a computer could be used to control the video signal - opened the door for the highly sophisticated video postproduction equipment of today. Current video postproduction is divided into two specific phases - off-line editing and on-line editing. Off-line editing is roughly analogous to cutting a film workprint. Just as cutting a workprint does not involve the master negative, off-line editing does not involve the master tape. The end result of an offline editing session is a list of decisions - expressed in SMPTE time code - indicating where cuts and splices should be made. The cut list is then taken to an on-line editing session and used as a guide for editing the master. It is in the on-line session that the original tape is cut - in an electronic sense only - and any special effects are executed and composited. As such, the online session can be considered the video equivalent to lab and optical work in film - only it is much faster. Virtually anything that can be done by an optical printer can be done electronically in an on-line session in a matter of minutes. But before the benefits of video postproduction can be applied to film, the film must first be transferred to the video format. At the dawn of the broadcast industry, the method used for transferring a film image to video was scarcely more sophisticated than shooting a film projector down the throat of a television camera. Because so much of the image was lost in the process, films were normally transferred only in completed form. In 1976, however, Rank-Cintel unveiled a remarkable filmto-tape transfer device that eliminated the traditional need for focusing lenses and a television camera. Called a flying spot scanner, the new device achieved a superior image by moving the film smoothly past the face of a cathode ray tube while an electron beam scanned the emulsion, video line by video line. The light that passes through each frame was broken up into its three primary colors - red, green and blue - and fed into three cathode ray pickup tubes that essentially converted the light into an electrical signal containing the information for color and brightness. The signal was then recorded onto videotape. With more accurate replication of colors, highlight details and shadows than its predecessors - and because of the crispness and clarity of the image - producers came to trust the Rank scanner and for the first time were able to reap the benefits of video editing. Special effects, however, were still a problem because the Rank was incapable of complete repeatability in register. Thus the elements of a composite did not always fit perfectly and often appeared to weave back and forth. In 1982, Composite Image Systems overcame the problem by fitting the Rank with a pin registration device. With pin registration, individual frames of the film negative are aligned precisely in a gate that engages pins into the sprocket holes and tightly pulls the frame into proper position for scanning. "The concept of pin registration has been used in the motion picture industry since it began," noted company president Joe Matza. "All film cameras have pin registration. We invented pin registered film-to-tape transfers for video by using the same printer movements as an optical printer. We do optical printing much the way a film effect house might, but we do our printing in an electronic medium. If the film is shot perfectly steady and without weave, we can replicate that on video. The importance of transferring accurately is that now your filmed originals can be composited electronically." Another advantage of the Composite Image Systems pin registered Rank is its ability to reposition the image during transfer with a combination of sixto-one zoom capability, preset aspect ratios and a joystick for moving along the vertical and horizontal axes. It is also capable of handling Vistavision film elements - the format of choice for Industrial Light and Magic. "A lot of people think Vistavision for television is absurd because it is so much larger than the television format, but the benefits of compositing images with Vistavision are tremendous. Since the format is so much larger than television format to begin with, when it is transferred the grain size in the film is automatically reduced by sixty percent. The result is a noticeably better image that displays more picture and less grain." A further advantage is that the system processes the video signal in component mode rather than composite mode. The composite video signal is the standard 525-line NTSC signal which is broadcast through cable and over the air to home receivers. A single composite signal contains both the luminance (brightness) and chrominance (color) information necessary to reproduce a picture on a monitor. Unfortunately, the dual nature of the signal has an inherent shortcoming in that video bandwidths were originally established on the basis of much narrower requirements for black-and-white transmission and could not be expanded to accommodate color. Eventually video engineers developed a means of putting the color information onto a high-frequency sub carrier which was interlaced onto the black-and-white signal much like two overlapping combs. The result was a compromise at best since it allows for some overlapping of the chrominance and luminance information in the encoding process, which in turn produces superfluous signal noise and flawed color fidelity. Rerecording the signal only magnifies the problem - as demonstrated by the inferior image quality of a pirated videocassette when compared to one purchased from the video store. With the red, green and blue thus isolated, it is unnecessary to have another signal for the luminance factor since brightness - in essence, white light - is actually the sum of the three primary colors. Though it is a superior signal, component video is still only an analog signal recorded onto magnetic tape - a dictate of equipment designed before the advent of current digital technology. Continuously varying - as evidenced visually by its familiar wavy trace on an oscilloscope - the analog signal is subject to distortion or degradation every time it is rerecorded. A digital signal, on the other hand, is represented by a precise series of numbers stored on a magnetic disk. Encoded and decoded with mathematical exactness, a digital recording system is fully capable of producing multigenerational copies indistinguishable from the original. All of this dovetails directly into the video strategy at Composite Image Systems. "Many companies composite video by running tape elements into a DDR." Matza explained. "We go one step further by converting the original film negative into RGB component format which is then fed into the DDR." The Abekas DDR - a digital disk recorder - is an essential compositing tool because of its unique ability to simultaneously play and record in the digital format. As such, the DDR employs two high-speed computer disk drives to store up to fifty seconds of film per disk, juggling effects elements back and forth between disks as the shot progresses. "A basic example of our approach would be a shot of the Enterprise in space. We would run the starfield background straight into the DDR for digital storage. Next we would take the bluescreen Enterprise footage and feed that into our Ultimatte system to derive a matte. Ultimatte locks in on the color blue and suppresses it electronically, turning the blue into black and becoming a key signal that will be used to electronically switch a background into the place of the suppressed bluescreen. At that point we have two signals - a black-and-white matte signal and a color signal of the Enterprise. Then we go to the DDR. First the starfield element is stored directly onto the first disk. Then we feed in the two signals containing the Enterprise and its matte. As the background is played back from the first disk, the second disk records both the background and the keyed foreground to a composite image. The process is repeated for each new element - such as engine glows, another ship or a planet. Layer after layer can be added by shifting the current stage of the composite from disk to disk - and because everything is recorded digitally, first generation quality is maintained throughout." The final composite is output to one-inch videotape and sent to Star Trek's live-action editor where it is joined to the rest of the episode in an on-line editing session. 'Since the entire series is transferred and edited on tape, it means our work is exactly equal to the first generation live-action footage. Working in the digital domain, there is no perceptible difference." Several blocks away from Composite Image Systems is The Post Group - the focal point of Star Trek's video effects - where an array of high-tech editing bays house the most advanced arsenal of video equipment ever assembled under one roof. The facility and its capabilities are the culmination of many years of dedication to video technology by chief operating officer Rich Thorne. "When I saw Star Wars," said Thorne, "that was it - I wanted to be George Lucas on video. When we started in 1976, the company was small and poor, and there was not much to work with because the technology did not exist. So I began hiring these weird special effects editors that understood 3-D space and motion. They were creative, but they also had enough technical knowledge to put the equipment together. In order to be competitive with film you have to have true 3-D capability. We were trying to imitate motion control with video." Producing video effects that looked like they might have been done on film was the unwavering objective of the aggressive young company - and before long, Thorne and associates were doing just that. "In the early days of video effects, our first inclination was to build everything electronically just because we had the equipment and it could be done. Sometimes that meant doing things the hard way, however." By the time Peter Lauritson had decided that video might be the solution to getting Star Trek off the ground, Thorne had begun to utilize film elements more and more in his quest for realistic electronic effects. The timing could not have been better, for it was The Post Group's successful test compositing of several old Enterprise elements from Star Trek III that ultimately won it the contract. "With Star Trek, we take a hybrid approach to the special effects. A staff member of The Post Group sits down with the producer and effects coordinators, and together they decide which elements should be originated on film and which ones would be better created electronically. For example, at one point Peter Lauritson considered creating the Enterprise from 3-D computer graphics. After preliminary testing, it was decided that the image was not quite convincing enough and that the computer rendering would have been just too time consuming for the schedule. So the ship was built as a model at ILM. Other effects, however, such as phasers or photon torpedoes, are fast and easy and look great when generated electronically." At The Post Group, two fully-equipped editing bays are reserved exclusively for use by the Star Trek effects team. Generally, Rob Legato supervises the activities in one while Dan Curry oversees the other. A Grass Valley 300 switcher is the central device in each bay, holding much the same position as an optical printer would in the realm of film. The switcher produces a variety of wipes, fades and dissolves. As its name implies, however, its primary function is to serve as a central switching point for all video signal sources available in the edit bay. In essence, it is a controlling, routing and mixing device that can integrate images from several sources to create a new one. After proving to everyone's satisfaction that the Enterprise would still boldly go where no one had gone before - even on video - the Star Trek effects team still had to replicate a

number of other familiar illusions. "For the transporter effect," revealed first season effects editor Fred Raimondi, "the old TV show used aluminum dust sprinkled in front of a spotlight. We thought we could do better than that, so Rob Legato designed a new effect and brought all the elements to me. He had done some full-screen animation of blue streaks that dropped into frame over a black background and also some full-screen animation of sparkles. He wanted to combine them into an effect that would last five seconds, creating the element that would comprise the actual 'beam in' effect." "Usually we do not use an element in its original state," Legato remarked. "We decided that the streaks needed more 'oompf - so we took the streak element and displaced it by five frames in the DDR, creating a two-layered streak. That looked promising so we did it again, creating a three-layered streak. We added the twinkles to the streak element by doing a soft-edge wipe between the two, using our switcher which has a built-in wipe function. The wipe tracked the edge of the streak element, replacing the streaks with sparkles. Once we were happy with the transition, we dubbed it from the DDR to oneinch tape, which became our master 'beam in' effect." Raimondi handled the actual hands-on manipulation as Legato directed the session. "First we generated the background plate of the crew members fading away by cross-dissolving between the full set and the empty set. Then we had our artist - Laurie Resnick - use the Quantel Paintbox to make articulate mattes with a soft edge. The Paintbox will accept live video from any source, enabling a single video frame to be painted with an electronic paintbrush. We can retouch any area using existing colors in the frame, or we can cut in any shade matte. For the transporter we used an airbrush-style function to create people mattes with a ghostly soft edge." A final subtle touch was devised to help blend the transporter effect into each live-action scene. With an Ampex Digital Optics - a device that manipulates flat video images in 3-D space - Raimondi was able to feed in the full-frame master transporter effect. "From there it was a relatively simple matter to position and rotate the ADO panel - which now contained the transporter effect - to fit over each actor individually, creating a sense of perspective and depth. As each shot progresses, a series of circular softedge wipes from the switcher is employed to manipulate the sparkles into various areas of the bodies." Though overused on low-budget commercials and football games, the ADO's ability to rotate and tilt a flat image stands it in good stead with Raimondi. "I used it to fit images into the viewscreen on the bridge of the Enterprise. In the old series, you saw the screen head-on or not at all. Using the ADO, I can fit an image into the viewscreen from virtually any angle or perspective on the set." The Quantel Mirage - an equally useful device in the editing bay - works along similar lines as the ADO, but with some significant differences. The Mirage blurs the boundaries between image manipulation and image synthesis, actually mapping input video onto a three-dimensional shape and then moving that shape through space in real time. "A lot of what we deal with are digital video effects," commented technical director Phil Mendelson. "This applies to real-time processing of an input video signal - like Mirage or ADO - whereas computer graphics would be the generation and manipulation of an image from scratch." Though the Mirage does not create images from scratch, it does allow for the creation of custom shapes via programming. "Basically what it does is hack the frame up into six thousand polygons that can then be manipulated into shapes," Raimondi noted. "The Mirage also treats time and space just like a computer graphics device, and it has one really nice feature that systems like the ADO do not have - lighting. The Mirage has six user definable light sources which allow the programmer to define the type of light, color, intensity and position of key lights, as well as the amount of ambient light on the subject." A powerful tool in the video arsenal, the Mirage is often called upon to manipulate film elements shot on stage for Star Trek, converting sometimes bland images into spectacular vistas or a majestic alien visage. Many of the Star Trek planets are created on the Mirage. "The Mirage can take a flat raster image and manipulate it into a preprogrammed shape. There are many possibilities - but in the case of a planet, of course, it would be a sphere. To create texture on that sphere, Dan Curry and Rob Legato would generally find an organic texture that actually exists - a rock formation or mudslide, for instance - and photograph it as a 35mm slide. From there it would be transferred to tape and used as a wraparound input source for the planet." Since most digital effects devices provide their own key signals, the Mirage is quite capable of cutting a hole in a starfield background to create its own composite. However, this function is rarely used for producing planet effects. "We all agreed that the matte edge was just too hard," Raimondi stated. "So since the Mirage shape is really nothing more than a circle, we decided to create a soft-edge white circle wipe on black using the switcher. We matched up the correct size and then fed everything into the DDR to create the final composite of our planet nestled in a sea of stars." The Mirage is also called upon frequently to create more complex images, and it is these instances that afford the effects editor an opportunity to exercise some creative input. "If the shot is a stock effect like a planet or ship flyby, there is not much room for discussion. But if it is a 'one time only' effect that revolves around a story point, then I could usually sit down with the effects supervisor for that episode and we would give ourselves about four hours to design and experiment with the effect." One of the more unusual effects to come out of such a session was the hitherto unseen Enterprise deflector shield. "I was in a cloth store," Curry explained, "and saw some slivers of silver mylar hanging on the wall in the shape of a hula skirt. It had a great shiny look, and I knew it would be good for something." Procuring some of the mylar and delivering it to the effects stage, Curry and Ron Moore wasted little time in putting it to use. By shooting through various diffusion filters and diffraction gratings, we were able to achieve a very prismatic look or a soft glowing quality." The mylar pom-pom footage was then attacked on the Mirage. "What the element looked like alone," said Raimondi, "was a crosshatch pattern of every color of the rainbow. We took that element and put it onto the Mirage sphere shape, but it looked too much like the original element. The phaser beam itself was created on the Quantel Harry - a digital paintbox device which can store 2400 frames on four very large disk drives. By accepting input from the switcher, the Harry can be used to step through a scene frame by frame while allowing an artist to wield an electronic paintbrush. Possessing a remarkable range of colors, styles of pen and artistic freedom, the Harry has the ability to rotoscope a scene while simultaneously allowing the artist to generate hand-drawn mattes or color animation that can be modified, removed or immediately composited as an effects shot. "Those little touches are what make it fun to work here," said Curry. "When we get a show in, there is little time to really go wild and do the kinds of things that video is capable of now. "The crossover was established in two shots," Legato recalled. "We started with Riker standing with his back to us in front of a holodeck door which opened to reveal the forest. He stepped out into the landscape and we cut to the reverse angle that revealed him standing amidst an entire forest with the doorway and Enterprise corridor situated behind him like a dimensional hole. The door closed and faded away, leaving Riker alone in the woods. Both shots were bluescreen video composites. Riker walked out and appeared to be standing on the ground, but in reality he stepped out of the doorway onto a frontlit bluescreen cyclorama. We had shot a background plate in the park and carefully measured the angle of the camera tilt and the lens height, which we then matched as closely as possible on the bluescreen stage. The hardest thing was matching the lighting, which is never easy. Until Star Trek, I had not done much bluescreen work entailing actors standing on the screen itself. The reason we were successful with it was because of the Ultimatte." An integral and absolutely necessary component in film quality video compositing, the Ultimatte system was invented by Petro Vlahos who was also responsible for developing the color difference bluescreen technique for motion pictures. "Until the late '70s," said Legato, "you had to composite video bluescreen by using chroma-key techniques in a switcher. Generally switchers can key off one of two signals in an image - either luminance or chroma. A switcher can take the strength of that signal and suppress it, turning it on or off. As with film bluescreen, you can isolate the actor in front of it and generate an electronic matte which allows you to 'key in' or combine a foreground with a background. That is typically what you see on the news every night. It is not very delicate though - in fact, it is pretty much an either/or situation - so you cannot do elegant composite work in chroma-key. A switcher has a clip point of 'yes' or 'no' - everything remotely blue is keyed out, which is called a non-additive mix. The Ultimatte works like film separations. It locks in on the color using RGB component signals and employs variable-density exposures to allow an additive mix. It will even hold a shadow cast onto the bluescreen - which we did with Riker in the holodeck scene. With Ultimatte, anything that has a difference between blue and green will be suppressed to black, but it will be done linearly. The shadow cast on the bluescreen is a darker area, so that darker area translates in a linear manner as to how much background is actually put over that black. It adds a background to the bluescreen; but where that blue is darker, it adds a darker background. Hence the shadow is still there. The ability to hold a shadow really marries Riker to the background, and you just cannot do that on film. The shadows would have to be animated in. Ultimatte will hold smoke and reflections in glass as well, which is very difficult for film." Not only was Riker matted into the scene, but the door and hallway in the reverse angle were likewise composite elements. "This was the pilot episode and they had not yet constructed a holodeck door with an adjacent hallway. So I shot the doorway with a bluescreen behind it. Then I shot the hallway separately and reduced it on the ADO to make it appear a bit longer. The corridor and door were matted together and then laid on top of the forest background plate. Riker was matted over the plate containing the door and we just cross-dissolved between the forest with the door and the forest with no door behind him." The Ultimatte has also been used to enhance the realism of routine bluescreen shots. "If there is a shiny table sitting in a room underneath a bluescreen window, we can easily take the window element, use the ADO to flip it upside-down and then print it into the table as a reflection. Shadows and reflections help a great deal in making an effect look more realistic, so the Ultimatte is an important tool here." Image G began its Star Trek tenure immediately after the pilot episode, producing new elements of the Enterprise as well as the Ferengi fighter ship supplied by Greg Jein and Dave Goldberg. The firm's capabilities as an effects house were well known to Rob Legato who had worked with Barron on several video-oriented commercials. "As a commercial effects house," stated Barron, "we are geared for fast turnaround on high-quality product - which is what we provide for Star Trek as well." To generate time- and cost-effective motion control shots of the Enterprise and the other assorted spacecraft, Image G utilizes a customized blend of film and video technology. "Most of the equipment we shoot Star Trek with is custom-built by our shop. We use a thirty-five-foot Ibeam track with an orthogonal camera mover. Our camera is a lightweight Cunningham with pin registered movement and Nikon lenses, and our motion control system was customdesigned for our applications by Bill Tondreau. One of our handier devices is a Sony CCD video assist fed into a JVC singleframe time-lapse recorder which allows us to tape moves and play them back for review. We also run the video assist into a Panasonic switcher and second tape player, allowing us to mix in the film backgrounds that are supplied by Star Trek. By doing that, we can preview the composites on stage to check positions and sizes and lighting by using the switcher mixes and splitscreens. Our stage cameramen - Erik Nash and Adrian Hurley - have really put the preview function to good use. For one episode, we had the new Enterprise fly into the background footage drydock used in Star Trek III - and what we wound up doing was running a tape of the movie and matching the moves and angles of the old ILM shot by using our split-screen comparison mix. We matched the interactive light as well. Like everything else, we shot the moves on the half-inch JVC video recorder and then ran the tape over to Rob and Dan who gave us suggestions and approval." Unlike the footage furnished by ILM, the model photography of Image G does not involve bluescreen. "We shoot our models frontlight-backlight. We turn out the beauty pass with all the production lighting and then relight and silhouette the ship to create a matte. All we have to do is set up just enough light behind the model to do the job and then 'light out' the model mount by placing a white paddle in front of the post and balancing the exposure on it to the backlight. This leaves the model apparently suspended against a field of light. We shoot both the beauty and matte passes on color film together on the same roll. The garbage mattes are generated on video. The Post Group and CIS are able to pull a luminance key off the blackand-white contrast rather than a chroma-key off the color. That allows them to control the quality of the matte which can be selectively set at the time of the transfer." The developments in video effects please Barron no end. But it is a new progression in motion control that holds the most excitement for Image G. "We have developed something that we hope to use in the third season of Trek- a real-time, liveaction-speed motion control camera. We call it the 'Bulldog' because it's large and scary. The thing will go eight feet per second on its track - which we screw into the stage floor. It uses two-and-a-half horsepower AC servo motors which allow very large camera moves but still have the ability to go back and do repeat passes. The track azimuth and elevation are one unit with all the servo motors nested together. We can attach various length boom sections to the elevation box - sections of six, eight or twenty feet. Hanging from the boom is a camera with a pan, tilt and zoom capability - so it simulates a Louma or Chapman crane, but with full repeatability. We feel it can open up a realm of new possibilities for Star Trek." Several additional companies provide auxiliary effects work from time to time, augmenting the video manipulation of The Post Group with contributions such as stop-motion from David Stipes Productions, animation from Stokes/Kohne Associates and matte paintings from Illusion Arts. At one point, The Post Group had toyed with creating matte paints on their own digital paintbox systems. "Our early results were disappointing," admitted Curry, "but recently we have had a lot of success with the Harry - due largely to the efforts of our visual effects animator Steve Price. Color blending on the Harry is not a problem because you can pull color from the principal tonality of whatever you are trying to match and use it to wash over an element from another source. In other words, you can take some gray rock artwork and cut and paste it electronically to extend a pile of brown rocks. Then you can sample the color of brown off the rocks and wash it over the gray rocks until a satisfactory blend is achieved. This sort of thing was possible before, but not with the level of finesse now available." With the help of talented people and cutting-edge technology, Curry and Legato continue to push for the improved marriage of video and film. "I have changed in this last TV season alone," admitted Curry. "When I started out here it was from a film effects man's point of view. Now I find myself breaking all the rules. I shot a matte painting directly onto video and it looked fine. I did a phaser zap where I mixed in a hobby store human skeleton model with some characters who get particularly nasty phaser hits - and I shot the skeleton directly onto video. Two years ago, that would have been anathema." 'Whatever works' has always been the credo of special effects. While the limits of video still remain unexplored, it would be incorrect to regard video as the final frontier. One hundred and fifty years ago, the science of capturing images on film was unknown. Less than sixty-five years ago, video existed only in the realm of science fiction stories. The laserdisk emerged only in the last decade. What new imaging medium awaits? The only certainty is that the next generation of special effects artists will be rolling up their sleeves and exploring its limits the moment it comes into being. "We wanted to take audiences on a completely different ride," observed producer Steven-Charles Jaffe about Brooksfilms' decision to shoot a sequel to their 1986 hit, The Fly, "It had to be a sequel in the class of Aliens, with more action involving the title character and the drama opened up a bit. We wanted to deliver more of everything on screen. The difficulty was that we had to do it with roughly the same amount of time and money as we had on the original." Adding to the difficulty was the fact that Brooksfilms was asking for 'sequel magic' without the guiding force of director David Cronenberg who had managed to take the first film's elements of gore and offbeat sentimentality and craft from them a uniquely powerful tale of obsession and love. Hoping to sustain the Cronenberg touch, Brooksfilms had approached the director regarding a possible sequel in mid-1987, but found him irrevocably committed to Dead Ringers. Stuart Cornfeld - producer of the original - had already tapped Chris Walas to expand upon his Oscarwinning makeup effects for The Fly II. When it became apparent that Cronenberg would not be available, Walas - eager to try his hand at directing - approached Cornfeld with the idea of helming the project himself. Walas knew the logistics of effects shooting and was arguably the one person from the original crew who could meet the stepped-up production requirements of the sequel and still keep within its modest $12 million budget. Acting on a strong endorsement from Cronenberg himself, Cornfeld signed Walas to direct and then stepped aside as producer to oversee a number of other projects. The sequel begins with Veronica Quaife giving birth to the son of the late Seth Brundle. Their offspring - who grows to maturity at a startlingly accelerated rate - is simultaneously blessed with his father's scientific intellect and cursed with a rapidly evolving set of housefly genes. Orphaned at birth, Martin Brundle (Eric Stoltz) is raised under the watchful eye of industrialist Anton Bartok (Lee Richardson) who has enshrined Brundle's telepod prototypes in a massive research facility but cannot get them to work. It is Bartok's devious intent to harness the genius of Martin to complete the monumental work begun by his father. Growing up in a sterile world of machines and circuit boards, Martin nonetheless manages to become romantically entwined with computer operator Beth Logan (Daphne Zuniga) just as his insect genes begin to assert themselves and trigger a physical metamorphosis. By the time Martin discovers the evil intent behind Bartok's solicitude, he has become the fully-transformed 'Martinfly' - complete with a thirst for revenge. Retreating into the dark recesses of the laboratory, the man-fly hatches a bloody plot to sacrifice his betrayer in a desperate attempt to restore his own humanity. "The difference between Martin's metamorphosis and the metamorphosis in the first movie," observed Chris Walas, "is that ours is a natural evolution rather than a physical decay. That in itself changes the overall dynamics of the story. Martin is growing from the first moment that he appears on screen to the last frame of the film. His body knows where it's going, but 24 < CINEFEX 37 CHRIS WALAS DIRECTOR

While Walas and Brooksfilms worked with a succession of writers to perfect the script, a small design crew from Chris Walas Incorporated launched into creature design work in October 1987. Facing them was the daunting tasks of creating a final-stage animatronic fly that was elegant yet sinister. Full preproduction began in November with the assembly of a crew of twenty-seven headed by project supervisor Jon Berg and shop supervisor Mark Walas. "While the original was basically a makeup show with our work coming in during the closing minutes," said Berg, "this time we were responsible for carrying the final third of the film. The audience would have to be carried along with the belief that our animatronic puppets were actual characters - not just the brief horrific outcome of a slow buildup initiated by an actor. In other words, we had to improve the mechanics of our effects sequences. This time Chris wanted full-figure shots of our bug creature, which meant the construction of one or more full-sized puppets. The rigs that made the various bugs move would have to be redesigned and the way we walked the fly in the first film had to be improved in order to save shooting time and facilitate setups. Worst of all was the fact that the climax of the film - when the fully-developed fly goes on a rampage in the Bartok lab - was constantly being rewritten. We did not know exactly what would be required until the very last minute - and even then the action in the script changed. This affected everything from bug and other animatronic effects to the makeup to even the freedom with which production designer Michael Bolton could build his sets." In the initial stages of preproduction, however, these obstacles were put aside in favor of developing the physical characteristics of Brundlefly's mutant offspring. Walas' demand that the creature be elegant and beautiful as well as menacing was a tall order. "Instead of hitting upon the ideal design out of the blue," said sculptor Howie Weed, "our bug evolved from the submission and revision of countless drawings and sculptures. A decision had been made early on that Martinfly was going to look more like an insect than the original Brundlefly, so we worked within certain guidelines - the head would be relatively small and the legs, trunk and arms would be very thin. This caused a good deal of aesthetic as well as mechanical difficulties. There were endless ways of making a creature with a small head and thin limbs look ludicrous, and perhaps only one or two ways of designing it so that it seemed impressive and deadly." The model unit - under Archie Ruff - worked hard and fast to complete the complicated fiberglass jigsaw arrangement of rock slabs that would make up the collapsible sea floor. A constant fear was that the sea floor would collapse with enough force to actually damage the Seacat model - of which there was only one - as it clung precariously to the lip of the cave opening. "The closer we came to disaster, the better it would look - but obviously we did not want to lose our precious model. The Seacat was twenty inches long and built purposely very heavy so that it would react well with the ocean floor it trundled across. Its caterpillar track treads were cast in solid white metal and really did look realistic, even from right up close." In all, the crew managed to complete more than twelve successful collapses. Other scenes of the Seacat were shot dry using overhead wire rigs - with particular attention being paid to matching the look of wet and dry photography. During the Seacat's exploration of the cave, the script called for eerie and unusual lifeforms to be viewed - both as a prime image and on video monitors. It was a perfect opportunity for classic OSF film work. "With the aid of the Micro-Zoom and the optical bench rigged for intense dark field illumination at very high magnification - up to one hundred power - we filmed a species of single-celled freshwater cilliate, a microscopic larval freshwater sponge and some amazingly eerie micro-droplets which looked like weird medutae as they glided past. On all of these we zoomed, rolled and faded in and out - and for the medutae, we overlaid oncoming particles to enhance the feeling of approach." In addition to the models and underwater sets, the effects team was responsible for several deep-sea explosions of varying sizes and strength. One of the most powerful came near the end of the film when the Deepstar station self-destructs. Years before, OSP had devised a technique - used in both Altered States and Supergirl- in which an explosion could be simulated by shooting highly magnified particles in water. Though the simulation would provide a powerful visual cue to correlate with sound effects, it would not result in the actual destruction of any portion of the set or models. "The beauty of the technique is that it provides the opportunity of trying numerous versions of the particulate explosion very inexpensively. The particles are filmed by pumping yeast granules towards the Micro-Zoom from a sixteenth-inch-diameter nozzle attached to a bulb or a header tank. Filmed at one frame per second and stained to whatever color is required, the particles are lit to further enhance the color with colored dark field illumination. The false perspective produced by the expanding jet of particles in water enhances the sense of scale. All that is then required is a good sound editor to finally draw together the sensory cues that tell the audience they are looking at one hell of a powerful event." By the time the Deepstar Six project was over, some 240 effects shots had been provided - almost four times the number originally storyboarded and budgeted! After twenty years, Oxford Scientific Films has come into its own as an acknowledged feature effects house. Of the original founders, only Peter Parks and Sean Morris still remain. However, the team has grown to include between thirty and forty employees and the original studio below Gerald Thompson's garden has been expanded five times over the years - culminating in the new studio completed in 1986. The partnership ongoing with Columbia will almost certainly lead to new challenges in the entertainment field. However, the shift from science to show business is by no means complete. The group continues to produce wildlife documentary material and continues also to maintain a stills library of over a quarter million images - mostly on biological and effects subjects. This continuing love for nature's organic wonders has, in fact, been directly responsible for OSF's remarkable evolution over the vears. "Our development of new hardware has really always been motivated by the desire to devise ever more creative ways of looking at reality and wildlife. Space-age technology, lasers and computers all provide optical tricks that are fantastic and impressive. But when I look at the strange and beautiful creatures that live underwater, I am still convinced that the very best special effects are found right there." In the early stages of production - before the principal models were constructed - the main unit needed video monitor footage of the Seacat vehicle on the edge of the collapsing sea floor. OSF complied by tossing together - in less than a day - a makeshift setting and a cardboard mockup of the craft that were then shot on film and transferred to video. / Suspended from a wire rig, the rescue craft dispatched from Deepstar Six is maneuvered into position over the imperiled Seatrack.
